title: Babies Nursed Longer When Their Mothers Took Garlic, and the Old Colic Worry Hasn't Held Up in Studies
text:
Babies Nursed Longer When Their Mothers Took Garlic, and the Old Colic Worry Hasn't Held Up in Studies
Nursing mothers have long been warned that garlic could upset their babies. A 1991 study found something closer to the opposite. When mothers took garlic, their milk smelled noticeably of it about two hours later, and their babies stayed at the breast longer and sucked more.
Julie Mennella and Gary Beauchamp of the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia reported the findings in Pediatrics. The work won the 2025 Ig Nobel Prize in Pediatrics, a research award that makes people laugh and then think, and it remains a reference point for anyone asking whether a mother's diet changes her milk.
The Garlic Smell Peaked About Two Hours Later
Mothers in the study took capsules containing either a placebo or garlic extract. According to the National Library of Medicine's LactMed database, the garlic dose was 1.5 grams, and mothers pumped small milk samples every hour for several hours. A panel of adults who did not know which samples came from which condition rated how strongly each smelled.
Garlic significantly and consistently increased the intensity of the milk's odor. The change was not evident at one hour, peaked at two hours, and then declined. LactMed attributes the smell to allyl methyl sulfide, a garlic compound that makes its way into milk. Other studies it summarizes found odor peaks roughly one to three and a half hours after mothers ate raw garlic.
The infants noticed. They stayed attached to the breast longer and sucked more when the milk smelled of garlic. They also showed a tendency to take in more milk, but that difference was not statistically significant. The authors suggested the amount of milk available may have limited how much more the babies could drink.
The Interest Faded with Repeated Garlic
A 1993 follow-up in Pediatric Research tested what happens when babies get garlic-flavored milk more than once. The researchers followed 30 mother-infant pairs on a bland diet, giving some mothers garlic for several days before a final garlic test session.
Infants with no prior exposure during the study fed longer when their mothers' milk smelled of garlic, about 48 minutes compared with about 38 minutes. Infants whose mothers had taken garlic repeatedly showed no change. Garlic did not significantly affect how often babies fed or how much milk they drank in any group.
That pattern suggests babies were responding to something new, not developing a taste for garlic.
Flavors Reach Babies Before and After Birth
Mennella later found that garlic eaten during pregnancy also changes the aroma of amniotic fluid, according to the Monell Center. The team chose garlic partly because earlier research had shown that dairy cows grazing on wild garlic produced milk with its aroma. "Yet at the time, it was widely believed that human milk should be bland," Mennella said in Monell's announcement.
Other substances, including vanilla, alcohol, and tobacco smoke, also reach breast milk. In a separate 1991 study in the New England Journal of Medicine, Mennella and Beauchamp found that alcohol flavored mothers' milk and that infants consumed significantly less milk after their mothers drank, contrary to the folk belief that alcohol helps nursing.
Mennella told The Philadelphia Inquirer that garlic shows up in milk a couple of hours after a mother eats it and clears about four to five hours after she stops eating it. Looking back, she said the study showed "one of the first ways we learn about foods is through what our mothers eat." Her advice to nursing mothers was simple: "Eat the healthy foods that you enjoy because your baby's going to learn about the food."
Colic Fears Have Not Been Backed by Studies
Garlic is often blamed for colic, but LactMed reports that two studies did not support the link. In a questionnaire study of 153 mothers, those who ate garlic were no more likely to report colic. In a blinded study, colic reports were similar after garlic and placebo.
Federal guidance is consistent with that. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says women generally do not need to limit or avoid specific foods while breastfeeding. Its main dietary cautions involve fish high in mercury and caffeine intake above about 300 milligrams a day.
The FDA considers garlic generally recognized as safe as a food flavoring, according to LactMed, though the database found no good scientific data on garlic alone as a way to increase milk supply.
The 1991 study was small and short, and it measured behavior during brief test sessions, not long-term feeding or growth. Research capsules also differ from garlic cooked into meals; LactMed notes that one study detected no garlic odor compounds in milk after mothers ate boiled garlic, while roasted garlic still produced an odor.
Concentrated garlic deserves more care. LactMed notes that garlic has anti-platelet effects, so women at risk of bleeding should use supplements cautiously. People allergic to garlic or related plants such as onion, leek, and chives should avoid it, and one nursing mother suffered severe breast burns after applying a raw garlic poultice for two days.
Parents who notice a baby fussing, refusing to feed, or showing signs of an allergic reaction should talk with a pediatrician or lactation consultant rather than cutting foods on their own.
Key Questions Answered
Does garlic change the smell of breast milk?
Yes. In the 1991 Pediatrics study, a blinded panel detected a stronger odor that peaked about two hours after mothers took garlic capsules.
How did babies react?
They stayed at the breast longer and sucked more. A trend toward drinking more milk was not statistically significant.
Does the effect last if mothers eat garlic often?
A 1993 follow-up found babies nursed longer only when garlic was new to them. Repeatedly exposed babies showed no change.
Does garlic cause colic?
Two studies summarized by the National Library of Medicine did not find a link between maternal garlic and infant colic.
Do breastfeeding mothers need to avoid garlic?
The CDC says mothers generally do not need to avoid specific foods. Garlic supplements may warrant caution for people at risk of bleeding.
Why did this study win an Ig Nobel Prize?
Its premise sounds amusing, but it showed early on that babies notice changes in breast milk flavor, which later research built on.
